docs.title: roman-lcs
docs.text: roman-lcs is a Python package designed for precision Pixel Response Function (PRF) and aperture photometry on time-series observations from the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope Wide Field Instrument (WFI). Developed as part of the TRExS (Transiting and Relativistic Exoplanet Search) project, it provides high-throughput photometry pipelines, local background subtraction, crowding metrics, and light curve extraction for both simulated and in-flight Roman observations.

docs.title: About NASA Roman & the Galactic Bulge Time Domain Survey
docs.text:
The Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope is NASA's new flagship observatory, engineered to explore the infrared universe with unprecedented speed and precision. Its primary imaging camera, the Wide Field Instrument (WFI), combines 18 Sensor Chip Assemblies (SCAs) totaling 300 megapixels to yield a 0.281 deg² field of view—roughly 100 times that of the Hubble Space Telescope at comparable resolution (0.11 arcsec/pixel).

A cornerstone community initiative of Roman is the Galactic Bulge Time Domain Survey (GBTDS). By continuously monitoring ~2 square degrees in the dense, dust-obscured Milky Way bulge with ~12-minute sampling over six 62-day seasons in the near-infrared, the GBTDS will detect tens of thousands of exoplanets via the transiting method, measure stellar variability across millions of light curves, and map Milky Way structure.

docs.title: The TRExS Project: Transits in the Roman Galactic EXoplanet Survey
docs.text:
TRExS (Transits in the Roman Galactic EXoplanet Survey) is a Wide Field Science initiative and a Roman Cycle 1 designed to maximize the transit science return from Roman's GBTDS. While the GBTDS is nominally optimized for gravitational microlensing, its high-cadence time-series imaging of hundreds of millions of stars toward the Galactic Center makes it one of the most powerful transiting exoplanet surveys ever conceived.

Key pillars of TRExS include: - Massive Exoplanet Yields: TRExS is predicted to discover between ~100,000 transiting exoplanets, expanding the catalog of known exoplanets by orders of magnitude compared to Kepler and TESS. - Statistical Demographics of Rare Systems: The enormous sample size places stringent demographic constraints on intrinsically rare planetary architectures, ultra-short-period planets, planets orbiting evolved or giant stars, and brown dwarf companions. - Galactic Depth & Diversity: Probing deep through the Galactic disk into the inner bulge, TRExS observes stars across diverse stellar populations, metallicities, and Galactic environments, mapping how planet occurrence varies throughout the Milky Way. - Near-Infrared Atmospheres: Leveraging Roman's near-infrared bandpass (WFI F146 and companion filters), TRExS enables direct atmospheric detection and thermal emission measurements (e.g., secondary eclipses and phase curves) for thousands of transiting giant planets at a population level. - Survey Synergy: By pairing transit discoveries with microlensing detections in the same survey footprint, Roman and TRExS will establish a unified census of planetary systems spanning orbital separations from <0.1 AU out to free-floating planets.

Because the Galactic bulge is intensely crowded, precision forward-modeling Pixel Response Function (PRF) photometry and crowd-aware aperture photometry are essential. roman-lcs delivers this photometry engine within TRExS, turning target cutouts from roman-cuts and ePSF models from roman-epsf into calibrated, high-precision light curves.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: roman-lcs requires Python ≥ 3.11.

docs.title: User Installation with pip
docs.text:
Install the latest release from PyPI:

pip install roman-lcs

Or install from a local clone:

git clone https://github.com/jorgemarpa/roman-lcs.git
cd roman-lcs
pip install -e .

docs.title: Development Installation with uv
docs.text:
We recommend uv for development. In development mode, roman-lcs links to local editable sibling checkouts of roman-cuts and roman-epsf:

# Clone the repository
git clone https://github.com/jorgemarpa/roman-lcs.git
cd roman-lcs

# Install all dependencies including development tools
uv sync --all-extras

# Run test suite
uv run pytest -v

# Run linting and type checking
uv run ruff check .
uv run mypy src/

# Build and preview documentation locally
uv run mkdocs serve

docs.title: Quickstart Guide
docs.text: roman-lcs provides both a Python API centered around LCExtractor and command-line tools for batch light curve extraction.

docs.title: 1. Simulated Images
docs.text: Simulated images are produced by the RImTimSim package. Cutouts prepared by roman-cuts are loaded directly into LCExtractor to fit the empirical or semi-analytical PRF model, subtract background, and evaluate multiple aperture radii.

docs.title: Python Quickstart
docs.text:
from roman_lcs import LCExtractor

# Step 1: Load time-series cutouts from an ASDF container created by roman-cuts
extractor = LCExtractor.from_asdf("target_cutout.asdf")

# Step 2: Perform PRF fitting and aperture photometry
extractor.fit_prf_photometry(
    targets=[0],               # Target star index in the catalog
    model_bkg=True,            # Model background scene
    do_aperture=True,          # Extract aperture photometry
    aperture_radius=3,         # Circular aperture radius in pixels
)

# Step 3: Export light curves and quality metrics to multi-extension FITS
extractor.to_fits("target_lightcurve.fits")

docs.text:
An example simulated full-frame image from RImTimSim:

Light curves are computed by fitting the PRF across every frame and saved into FITS files:

docs.title: 2. Roman Commissioning Data (ROMCOM)
docs.text: roman-lcs seamlessly extracts light curves from Roman Commissioning observations using cutouts generated by roman_cuts.com and ePSF models generated by roman-epsf.

docs.title: Python API for Commissioning Data
docs.text:
from roman_lcs import LCExtractor

# 1. Load commissioning cutout cube (multi-extension ASDF with GWCS metadata)
extractor = LCExtractor.from_asdf("com_target_cutouts.asdf")

# 2. Attach an ePSF model (built from roman-epsf or stpsf)
extractor.set_prf_model("roman_epsf_sca02_F146.fits")

# 3. Fit PRF and compute aperture photometry with multiple aperture radii
extractor.fit_prf_photometry(
    targets=[0],
    model_bkg=True,
    do_aperture=True,
    aperture_radius=[2.0, 3.0, 4.0],
)

# 4. Save calibrated light curve with photometric precision metrics (RMS, P2P, CDPP)
extractor.to_fits("com_target_lightcurve.fits")

docs.title: Command-Line Tools
docs.text:
roman-lcs includes command-line scripts for single and batch pipeline execution:

# Single target extraction
roman-lc-extract \
    --input com_target_cutouts.asdf \
    --output com_target_lightcurve.fits \
    --prf-file roman_epsf_sca02_F146.fits \
    --aperture-radius 3.0

# Batch extraction over directories (suitable for HPC / SLURM arrays)
roman-lc-extract-batch \
    --input-dir ./cutouts/ \
    --output-dir ./lightcurves/ \
    --prf-file roman_epsf_sca02_F146.fits \
    --max-workers 8

docs.title: Output FITS Data Structure
docs.text: The generated FITS files contain: - PRIMARY Header: Comprehensive metadata including target coordinates (RA, Dec), SCA ID, filter, observing program, cadence count, and pipeline version. - EXT 1 (Binary Table): Time-series photometry columns: - TIME: Barycentric Julian Date / frame epoch - PSF_FLUX, PSF_FLUX_ERR: Optimal PRF-fitted flux and uncertainty - APERTURE_*_FLUX, APERTURE_*_FLUX_ERR: Aperture fluxes across configured radii - CROWDSAP: Crowding metric (ratio of target flux to total flux in aperture) - FLFRCSAP: PRF flux fraction enclosed within the aperture mask - CENTROID_X, CENTROID_Y: Fitted sub-pixel centroid coordinates - QUALITY: Data quality flag bitmask

docs.title: compute_CROWDSAP
docs.text:
compute_CROWDSAP(
    psf_models, aperture_mask, idx=None, flux_weights=None
)

Compute the ratio of target flux relative to flux from all sources within the photometric aperture (i.e. 1 - Crowdedness). Follows definition by Kinemuchi et al. 2012: CROWDSAP = sum_{p in aperture} F_target(p) / sum_{p in aperture} F_total(p)

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default psf_models csr_matrix or ndarray

Matrix with the PSF models for all targets in the scene. It has shape [n_sources, n_pixels].

required aperture_mask ndarray

Array of boolean indicating the aperture for the target source. It has shape of [n_sources, n_pixels] or [n_pixels].

required idx int

Source index for which the metric is computed. Value has to be between 0 and psf_models first dimension size. If None, it returns the metric for all sources.

None flux_weights ndarray

Array of flux estimates for each source with shape [n_sources]. If provided, psf_models will be weighted by these fluxes before computing metrics.

None

Returns:

Name Type Description CROWDSAP ndarray or float

Crowdedness metric

required

Completeness metric

docs.title: correct_aperture_flux
docs.text:
correct_aperture_flux(
    flux: ndarray,
    flux_err: ndarray,
    flfrcsap: ndarray,
    crowdsap: ndarray,
) -> Tuple[ndarray, ndarray]

Correct aperture flux and flux error for contamination (crowding) and enclosed flux fraction.

Formulas: flux_removed = flux - (1 - crowdsap) * np.nanmedian(flux) flux_corr = flux_removed / flfrcsap flux_err_corr = flux_err / flfrcsap

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default flux ndarray

Raw aperture flux array.

required flux_err ndarray

Raw aperture flux uncertainty array.

required flfrcsap ndarray

Fraction of target flux enclosed in the aperture (completeness).

required crowdsap ndarray

Ratio of target flux to total flux in the aperture (crowding metric).

required

Returns:

Name Type Description flux_corr ndarray

Aperture flux corrected for crowding and flux completeness.

flux_err_corr ndarray

Corresponding corrected flux uncertainties.

docs.title: make_snr_optimal_aperture
docs.text:
make_snr_optimal_aperture(
    signal: ndarray,
    error: ndarray,
    sat_flux: float = 60000.0,
    plot: bool = False,
) -> ndarray

Generate an optimal photometric aperture mask by maximizing the cumulative Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR).

The optimal aperture is determined by finding the pixel count that maximizes the total SNR or where the SNR improvement flattens out, ensuring that heavily saturated pixels are always enclosed before the cutoff is applied.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default signal ndarray

Array representing the estimated target flux or PRF model per pixel in electrons/sec.

required error ndarray

Array of the corresponding flux errors (e.g., background and Poisson noise) per pixel.

required sat_flux float

Flux threshold above which pixels are considered saturated. Defaults to 6e4.

60000.0 plot bool

If True, generates a diagnostic plot showing the cumulative SNR curve and the selected optimal pixel count cutoff. Defaults to False.

False

Returns:

Name Type Description optimal_mask ndarray

A boolean mask of the same shape as the input signal, where True indicates that a pixel is included in the optimal aperture.

docs.title: optimize_aperture
docs.text:
optimize_aperture(
    psf_model,
    target_complete=0.9,
    target_crowd=0.9,
    max_iter=100,
    percentile_bounds=[0, 100],
    quiet=False,
)

Function to optimize the aperture mask for a given source.

The optimization is done using scipy Brent's algorithm and it uses a custom loss function goodness_metric_obj_fun that uses a Leaky ReLU term to achive the target value for both metrics.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default psf_model csr_matrix

Sparse matrix with the PSF models for all targets in the scene. It has shape [n_sources, n_pixels].

required target_complete float

Value of the target completeness metric.

0.9 target_crowd float

Value of the target crowdeness metric.

0.9 max_iter int

Numer of maximum iterations to be performed by the optimizer.

100 percentile_bounds tuple

Tuple of minimun and maximun values for allowed percentile values during the optimization. Default is the widest range of [0, 100].

[0, 100]

Returns:

Name Type Description optimal_percentile ndarray

An array with the percentile value to defines the "optimal" aperture for each source.

docs.text:
from_file(
    fname: Union[str, List[str], ndarray],
    cutout_size: int = 32,
    cutout_center: Union[
        Tuple[float, float], Tuple[int, int]
    ] = (0, 0),
    sources: Optional[DataFrame] = None,
    file_version: str = "1.0",
    **kwargs,
) -> LCExtractor

Reads data from files and initiates a new object of LCExtractor class. Two options are available: 1. If providing pixel coordinates with cutout_origin, the data will be fixed tothe pixel grid, no dithering correctin will be applied and the star field will move across the image. 2. When providing cutout_center in RA, Dec coordinates, the data will be cetered in the target coordinate and account for dithering. The star field will be fixed, but the pixel grid will change.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default fname str or list of strings

File name or list of file names of the FFI files.

required cutout_size int

Size of the cutout in pixels, assumed to be squared.

32 cutout_center tuple of floats

Center of the cutout in RA, Dec coordinates. If provided, the cutout will be centered on this position and the pixel grid will be adjusted to account for dithering.

(0, 0) sources DataFrame

Catalog with sources to be extracted by PSFMachine

None **kwargs dictionary

Keyword arguments that defines shape model in a Machine class object. See psfmachine.Machine for details.

{}

Name Type Description LCExtractor Machine object

A Machine class object built from the FFI.

docs.text:
plot_prf_model(
    ax: Optional[Axes] = None,
    hires: bool = False,
    stretch: str = "linear",

Plot the Point Response Function (PRF) model for the current LCExtractor instance.

docs.title: compute_p2p_scatter
docs.text:
compute_p2p_scatter(
    flux: ndarray,
    time: Optional[ndarray] = None,
    normalize: bool = False,
    ppm: bool = False,
) -> float

Compute the point-to-point ($\sigma_{\text{P2P}}$) scatter of a light curve.

The point-to-point scatter is calculated using: $$\sigma_{\text{P2P}} = \frac{1.4826}{\sqrt{2}} \text{MAD}(\Delta y)$$ where $\Delta y$ is the difference between consecutive points in the flux or magnitude time-series, and $\text{MAD}(\Delta y)$ is the median absolute deviation of $\Delta y$: $$\text{MAD}(\Delta y) = \text{median}(|\Delta y - \text{median}(\Delta y)|)$$

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default flux ndarray

Flux or magnitude time-series array.

required time ndarray

Time values corresponding to the cadences. If provided, observations are sorted by time before computing consecutive differences.

None normalize bool

If True, normalize by the median flux (dimensionless relative scatter).

False ppm bool

If True, normalize by the median flux and express in parts-per-million (ppm). Overrides normalize.

False

Returns:

Name Type Description p2p_scatter float

Point-to-point scatter $\sigma_{\text{P2P}}$.

docs.title: sparse_lessthan
docs.text:
sparse_lessthan(
    arr: spmatrix, limit: Union[float, ArrayLike]
) -> spmatrix

Compute less than operation on sparse array by evaluating only non-zero values and reconstructing the sparse array. This function return a sparse array, which is crutial to keep operating large matrices.

Notes: when doing x < a for a sparse array x and a > 0 it effectively compares all zero and non-zero values. Then we get a dense boolean array with True where the condition is met but also True where the sparse array was zero. To avoid this we evaluate the condition only for non-zero values in the sparse array and later reconstruct the sparse array with the right shape and content. When x is a [N * M] matrix and a is [N] array, and we want to evaluate the condition per row, we need to iterate over rows to perform the evaluation and then reconstruct the masked sparse array.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default arr sparse

Sparse array to be masked, is a 2D matrix.

required limit (float, array)

required

docs.title: threshold_bin
docs.text:
threshold_bin(
    x: ArrayLike,
    y: ArrayLike,
    z: ArrayLike,
    z_err: Optional[ArrayLike] = None,
    abs_thresh: int = 10,
    bins: int = 15,
    statistic: Callable = nanmedian,
) -> Tuple[ndarray, ndarray, ndarray, ndarray, ndarray]

Function to bin 2D data and compute array statistic based on density. This function inputs 2D coordinates, e.g. X and Y locations, and a number value Z for each point in the 2D space. It bins the 2D spatial data to then compute a statistic, e.g. median, on the Z value based on bin members. The statistic is computed only for bins with more than abs_thresh members. It preserves data when the number of bin memebers is lower than abs_thresh.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default x ndarray

Data array with spatial coordinate 1.

required y ndarray

Data array with spatial coordinate 2.

required z ndarray

Data array with the number values for each (X, Y) point.

required z_err ndarray

Array with errors values for z.

None abs_thresh int

Absolute threshold is the number of bib members to compute the statistic, otherwise data will be preserved.

10 bins int or list of ints

Number of bins. If int, both axis will have same number of bins. If list, number of bins for first (x) and second (y) dimension.

15 statistic callable()

The statistic as a callable function that will be use in each bin. Default is numpy.nanmedian.

nanmedian

Returns:

Name Type Description bin_map ndarray

2D histogram values

new_x ndarray

Binned X data.

new_y ndarray

Binned Y data.

new_z ndarray

Binned Z data.

new_z_err ndarray

BInned Z_err data if errors were provided. If no, inverse of the number of bin members are returned as weights.

Converts the light curve to a FITS file in the Kepler/TESS file format.

False extra_data dict

Extra keywords or columns to include in the FITS file. Arguments of type str, int, float, or bool will be stored as keywords in the primary header. Arguments of type np.array or list will be stored as columns in the first extension.
